source: វិធានការចម្រុះគ្រប់គ្រងដំណាំ លើដំណាំស្រូវ (Integrated Pest Management on Rice), training slide deck, Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries of Battambang province, presented by Ms. Yem Sophy, Oct 20, 2017 (contact: ysophy168@gmail.com, 012 558 312)
text: Rice bug (Leptocorisa oratorius) is a slender, long-legged bug that pierces developing (milk-stage) grains and sucks out the milky contents, leaving the grain empty, discolored, or malformed; it is most damaging from flowering through the milk stage of grain fill, and less so once grains harden. Adults feed most actively at dawn and dusk and hide in shaded, cooler spots (like grassy field edges) during the heat of the day. A female can lay roughly 250-300 eggs, typically in rows of about 2-3 along a leaf. Rice bug carries a strong odor, characteristic of stink bugs; the deck notes that around 80% of milk-stage feeding damage occurs in the first roughly week after grain emergence, when grains are softest, dropping off sharply as grains harden. Recorded natural enemies include scelionid egg-parasitic wasps and several damselfly species preying on nymphs and adults, plus a general predatory-beetle guild feeding on eggs and young nymphs.
